memoryText: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Today there is no new reading. Today is for review and reflection on what you have learned in Unit 10.

Begin by memorizing the verse above if you have not already. Say it aloud several times, then try writing it from memory. These verses have been the anchor of this unit, and they sum up the instruction of the wisdom books.

“Trust in the LORD with all your heart.” Wisdom begins with trust, not with technique. In Proverbs, we saw that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. Trust is the same posture seen from the inside. We believe that God is good and that he knows what he is doing.

“And do not lean on your own understanding.” Ecclesiastes shows what happens when we do. The Preacher explored the world with all his intelligence and found it a vapor. Psalm 73 shows a man who nearly fell because he trusted what he saw. The way that seems right to a man ends in death. Our understanding is not useless, but it cannot be our final authority.

“In all your ways acknowledge him.” Not only in church, but in work, money, marriage, friendships, speech, and decisions. This is the lived side of wisdom: bringing God into everything.

“And he will make straight your paths.” This is a promise. It does not say the path will be easy. It says that God will direct it. The Song of Solomon reminds us that his love is stronger than death. The Preacher ends with fear God and keep his commandments. The Psalms say that God holds our right hand.

Think of Christ, who trusted the Father perfectly and did not lean on his own understanding, and who is himself the wisdom of God. In him, the paths of all who trust are made straight.
unitRecap:
In Unit 10 you have read the wisdom books of the Old Testament: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Solomon, along with Psalms 19, 45, 49, 73, and a long journey through Psalm 119. If the story of Israel’s history showed how God rules his people, these books show how to live in the world God made.

Proverbs opened with the fear of the LORD as the beginning of knowledge, and called the reader to choose between the way of Wisdom and the way of Folly. You read the father’s instruction to his son, the warnings about adultery, laziness, and bad company, and the beautiful alternative of faithful love. You read Wisdom’s own speech in chapter 8, where she stands beside God at creation, a poetic picture that the New Testament sees fulfilled in Christ. You read hundreds of sayings on speech, work, friendship, justice, generosity, and pride, and saw that God holds human plans in his hand. The book ended with Agur’s humility and the portrait of the excellent wife, whose praise rests on the fear of the LORD.

Ecclesiastes asked the hard questions. The Preacher looked at life under the sun and found it a breath. He tried pleasure, work, and wisdom, and found that death comes to all. Yet he did not despair. He called us to receive life as a gift from God, to enjoy and to work, and to remember that God will bring every deed into judgment. His conclusion was simple: fear God and keep his commandments. Psalms 49 and 73 gave the hope the Preacher could only glimpse: God will ransom the soul from Sheol, and he himself is our portion.

The Song of Solomon celebrated love between husband and wife as a good gift from God, and a picture of the love between Christ and his church. Its great declaration was that love is strong as death. Psalm 119 offered a long meditation on the word of God as a lamp, honey, and light. And Psalm 45 closed the unit with the royal wedding.

Together these books teach that God is not only the Lord of history but the Lord of ordinary life. They also leave us longing for the one in whom all wisdom dwells.

reviewQuestions.question: What is the “fear of the LORD” and why is it the beginning of wisdom?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Look back at Proverbs 1:7, 9:10, and the closing of Ecclesiastes. The fear of the LORD is reverent trust: taking God seriously as God. Write a few sentences describing what it means, and how it differs from terror. Why is it the starting point rather than an add-on? How does the cross show both the reason to fear and the reason to trust?

reviewQuestions.question: How does Ecclesiastes’s conclusion answer the problem of vanity?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Recall the Preacher’s long exploration of work, pleasure, wealth, and wisdom, and his verdict that all is a breath. Then recall his final words: fear God and keep his commandments, for God will bring every deed into judgment. Write about how this conclusion answers the problem. Where is the hope in the book, and where does it point beyond itself to Christ?

reviewQuestions.question: How does Wisdom in Proverbs 8 point us toward Christ?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Look at Proverbs 8:22-31, where Wisdom speaks of being beside God as a master workman at creation. Compare it with John 1:1-3, Colossians 1:15-17, and 1 Corinthians 1:24. Write a few sentences on how the New Testament reads this passage, and what it means that Christ is the wisdom of God. How does this change how you seek wisdom?

reviewQuestions.question: What is the Song of Solomon ultimately about, and how should we read it?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Think about the Song as a celebration of married love, and then about the church’s long tradition of seeing in it a picture of Christ and his people. Look at Ephesians 5:25-32. Write a few sentences on how both readings can be held together. What does the Song teach about the goodness of desire, the value of covenant, and the strength of love?

prayerPrompts: Thank God for what the wisdom books have taught you.
Tell him where you still lean on your own understanding.
Ask him to keep the unit verse before you.
